1.title: Automation, Orchestration and AI in Operations
1.text: Welcome to Module sixteen: Automation, Orchestration and A I in Operations. It covers the exam area Security Operations. Each part of this module comes from the study notes of the same name, so you can read the notes after you watch.

1.title: What You Will Learn
1.text: By the end of this module you will be able to do six things. Automation and orchestration. Use cases. Considerations. A I in security operations. Intended outcomes and Sec Ops. Practice with exam-style questions and a recall check.

1.title: Where This Fits in the Exam
1.text: Here is where this module sits in the exam. Exam area: Security Operations (twenty-seven percent). Exam format: up to ninety questions in ninety minutes; a score of seven hundred fifty on a scale of one hundred to nine hundred passes. Validated against: the official Comp T I A Security plus S Y zero eight oh one V eight exam objectives.

1.title: Automation and orchestration
1.text: Automation and orchestration. Automation. Meaning: A single task runs without manual steps. Example: A script that disables a leaver's account. Orchestration. Meaning: Many automated tasks and tools are coordinated into one workflow. Example: Alert arrives, enrich the I P address, open a ticket, isolate the host, notify the owner. soar. Meaning: Security orchestration, automation, and response: a platform for this. Example: A playbook that handles phishing reports.

1.title: Automation and orchestration, continued
1.text: Automation and orchestration. The figure shows this: Orchestration links tools: detection, enrichment, ticket, containment, notification.

1.title: Use cases
1.text: Use cases. User provisioning. Accounts created and removed consistently. Resource provisioning. Servers and cloud resources built from templates. Desired state management. Systems return to the approved configuration automatically. Anomaly detection. Unusual behavior is flagged automatically. Ticket management. Tickets are created, updated and routed automatically.

1.title: Considerations (what can go wrong)
1.text: Considerations (what can go wrong). Guardrails. Limits that stop automation from doing harm (approvals, scopes, rate limits). Automation logic. Rules must be correct and tested; a bug is repeated at speed. Process engineering. Design the process well before automating it. Complexity. More moving parts to maintain and secure. Financial. Tool and maintenance costs. Process risks. A wrong action can spread quickly across many systems. Deployment. Roll out gradually and monitor. Exam tip: Automating a bad process just makes mistakes faster. Use guardrails and human approval for high-impact actions. Orchestration coordinates many tools; automation is one task.

1.title: AI in security operations
1.text: A I in security operations. Agentic A I. A I that plans and takes actions with tools toward a goal (for example investigating an alert). Chatbot. A conversational interface to ask for help, summaries or queries. Predictive analysis. Uses data to forecast problems or threats. A I-augmented baselines. A I helps learn normal behavior so abnormal behavior stands out. A I helps most when it assists analysts; humans stay accountable and verify results (module eight risks: hallucinations, prompt injection, data leaks).

1.title: Intended outcomes and SecOps
1.text: Intended outcomes and Sec Ops. Efficiency and time saving. Less manual work. Enforcing baselines. Systems stay at the approved configuration. Continuous improvements. Learn from results and refine. Productivity improvements. Analysts focus on hard problems. Reduced downtime. Faster detection and repair. Increased proactivity. Fix issues before users notice. Sec Ops blends security and operations. C I or C D (continuous integration and continuous deployment) builds, tests and releases code automatically, so security checks (secrets scanning, static analysis) can be built into the pipeline. Workflows use automation and integrations between tools through A P Is. Exam tip: If a question mentions coordinating many tools into one workflow, the answer is orchestration (soar); one task is automation.

1.title: Intended outcomes and SecOps, continued
1.text: Intended outcomes and Sec Ops. The figure shows this: Security checks inside a C I or C D pipeline: commit, scan, build, test, deploy. Exam tip: In a C I or C D pipeline, add secrets scanning and static analysis early ("shift left"). Agentic A I takes actions, so apply least privilege and approval gates to the tools it can use.

1.title: Practice Question 1
1.text: Question one. Fabrikam Outdoors wants a phishing report to trigger enrichment of the sender, a ticket, quarantine of the email and a notice to the reporter, all without manual steps. Which approach fits? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A: Orchestration with a soar playbook. Coordinating several tools and steps into one workflow is orchestration, usually done in a soar platform.

1.title: Practice Question 2
1.text: Question two. A team wants an automated task that disables an account when H R marks a worker as terminated. Which use case is this? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B: User provisioning and deprovisioning. Automatically creating and removing accounts is a user provisioning use case.

1.title: Practice Question 3
1.text: Question three. An automation script mistakenly isolates four hundred production servers within seconds. Which control would have limited the damage? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A: Guardrails such as approval and scope limits. Guardrails limit the scope and impact of automated actions.

1.title: Practice Question 4
1.text: Question four. An A I assistant can investigate an alert by running queries and opening tickets on its own. Which capability is this? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D: Agentic A I. An A I that plans and takes actions with tools toward a goal is agentic.

1.title: Practice Question 5
1.text: Question five. A pipeline should stop a build if a developer commits a password. Which control belongs in the C I or C D pipeline? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D: Secrets scanning. Secrets scanning in the pipeline catches credentials before release.

1.title: Practice Question 6
1.text: Question six. Systems are checked daily and any that drift are reset to the approved configuration automatically. Which use case is this? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D: Desired state management. Returning systems to an approved configuration automatically is desired state management.

1.title: Recall Check 1
1.text: Recall check one. Say each answer out loud before you listen to mine. Question one. What is the difference between automation and orchestration? Answer: Automation runs one task without manual steps; orchestration coordinates many tasks and tools. Question two. What does soar stand for? Answer: Security orchestration, automation, and response. Question three. What is a guardrail? Answer: A limit that stops automation from causing harm.

1.title: Recall Check 2
1.text: Recall check two. Say each answer out loud before you listen to mine. Question four. Name two use cases of automation in security. Answer: For example user provisioning and desired state management. Question five. What is agentic A I? Answer: A I that plans and takes actions with tools toward a goal. Question six. What does C I or C D stand for? Answer: Continuous integration and continuous deployment.

1.title: Module Recap
1.text: Here is the recap. Concepts: automation equals one task; orchestration equals many tools in a workflow; soar platform. Use cases: user and resource provisioning, desired state, anomaly detection, ticket management. Considerations: guardrails, logic, process engineering, complexity, cost, process risk, gradual deployment. A I: agentic, chatbot, predictive analysis, A I-augmented baselines; humans verify. Outcomes: efficiency, baselines, continuous improvement, productivity, less downtime, proactivity; security in C I or C D. In the next module, we continue the course.
